Annual Meetings

Morning Session - 2007 Meeting

Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger discuss the possibility of a credit crisis and the opportunities it might create as Buffett discounts the threat of subprime mortgage defaults as a "huge anchor" for the economy. Buffett also explains why he "outsourced" his philanthropy to the Gates Foundation, and calls gambling a "tax on ignorance."

Sat, May 5 2007 • 9:00 AM EDT
Key Chapters —
  1. 1. Jimmy Buffett sings "Berkshire Hathaway-ville"
  2. 5. Buffett sees no private equity "bubble" about to burst
  3. 9. "Extraordinary" things can happen when people panic
  4. 13. "Gambling is a tax on ignorance"
  5. 22. Buffett and Munger differ on climate change
  6. 28. Subprime mortgage defaults won't be "huge anchor"

4. Q1 earnings are "good"

WARREN BUFFETT: Just one or two items of business the â before we start the questioning.

Sync Video to Paragraph

We did report our earnings yesterday after the close, and I can't see the â are they up on the monitor?

Sync Video to Paragraph

But it was a good first quarter. We had a good year last year. The insurance earnings are going to go down. There's no question about that. How much they go down depends on Mother Nature and a few other factors.

Sync Video to Paragraph

But it's been an extraordinary period for insurance. I mean, nothing bad happened last year, and the same was true in the first quarter.

Sync Video to Paragraph

As you might expect, that favorable experience has caused people to lower prices in some areas quite dramatically. And the nature of insurance, if you write a one-year contract, say, six months ago, you were still getting premium at the old rate, if you write at a one-year policy, for another six months.

Sync Video to Paragraph

So there's a lag effect when things are getting either better or worse. And the lag effect from this point forward, we will â our insurance rates results will show the effect of lower prices.

Sync Video to Paragraph

They will probably show â certainly we have the most benign hurricane season imaginable last year. We have less hurricane exposure that we've written this year but, nevertheless, as natural catastrophes occur we will be paying out lots of money if and when they occur.

Sync Video to Paragraph

It couldn't get any better than it was last year from our standpoint. So things in the insurance world, our insurance earnings, underwriting earnings, are bound to decrease.

Sync Video to Paragraph

Now, what we really hope over time is more or less to break even on the underwriting of insurance. So when you see a significant profit like last year or underwriting profit this year, just look at that as kind of the good side of what will later be an offset to it in a way of an underwriting loss.

Sync Video to Paragraph

But if we break even in insurance on underwriting, we do very, very well because we generate lots of float and we earn money on that float and our float is at an all-time high.

Sync Video to Paragraph

So this is really the frosting on the cake when we have an underwriting profit, and it's not to be expected to necessarily â well, it won't occur year after year. Ever since we've been in the insurance business, about half the years we've made money underwriting and half we haven't.

Sync Video to Paragraph

I think our mix of business now is such that we'll even maybe do a touch better than that in the future, but we won't do anything like what we did in the last year and in the first quarter this year.

Sync Video to Paragraph

There's one unusual item in our balance sheet that you should be aware of. March 31, you'll see our receivables went up by about $7 billion. That was because of the Equitas transaction I described in the annual report.

Sync Video to Paragraph

On March 31st, the deal, basically, was closed at the end of the quarter. So we had a receivable of 7 billion, and then a couple of days later we were given 7 billion of cash and securities. So that receivable very quickly turned into liquid assets, cash.

Sync Video to Paragraph

And we sold all those securities we got. So we had 7 billion transferred from receivables to cash very early in April.

Sync Video to Paragraph

Other than that, most of our noninsurance businesses did fine. The residential construction-related businesses are getting hit, in some cases getting hit very hard, and in some cases getting just â but still reflecting decreases in their business.

Sync Video to Paragraph

And my guess is that that continues, perhaps, for quite a while. So you will see lower earnings coming from the companies that are related to residential construction such as Shaw, Johns Manville, ACME Brick, and that group.

Sync Video to Paragraph

But overall, compared to the companies they compete with, our managers continue to do an absolutely sensational job.

We have the greatest group of managers and, for that matter, we've got the greatest group of stockholders, of any company I know of in the world, and Charlie and I are very grateful.

AUDIENCE MEMBER: OK. First, given the ocean of equity money that is out there â private equity money â that is out there today chasing deals, and with the quality of the deals continually diminishing as the quantity of good deals continues to go down, and given the fact that these private equity funds are getting their equity portion of the money from pension funds and college endowments and using very high levels of borrowed money from the banks, this has the look, feel, and smell of a bubble that is about to burst and is likely to end badly for many of the deal-makers and the investors.

Sync Video to Paragraph

What events, in your opinion, could cause this bubble to burst, and how do you think this is likely to all end?

Sync Video to Paragraph

WARREN BUFFETT: Well, as you were reading off that list, we are competing with those people, so I started to cry as you â (laughs) â explained the difficulty we have in finding things to buy.

Sync Video to Paragraph

The nature of the private equity activity is such that it really isn't a bubble that bursts.

Sync Video to Paragraph

Because if you're running a large private equity fund and you lock up $20 billion for five or longer years and you buy businesses which are not priced daily, as a practical matter, the plug will not â even if you do a poor job, it's going to take many years before the score is put up on the score board, and it takes many years, in most cases, for people to get out of the private equity fund even if they wished to earlier.

Sync Video to Paragraph

So it does not â it's not like a lot of leverage can lead to in-marketable securities or something there. And the investors can't leave and the scorecard is lacking for a long time.

Sync Video to Paragraph

What will slow down the activity â or what could slow down the activity â is if yields on junk bonds became much higher than yields on high-grade bonds.

Sync Video to Paragraph

Right now the spread between yields on junk bonds and high-grade bonds is down to a very low level, and history has shown that periodically that spread widens quite dramatically.

Sync Video to Paragraph

That will slow down the deals, but it won't cause the investors to get their money back.

Sync Video to Paragraph

There's one other aspect, of course, that â of this frenzied activity, you might say, in private equity is that if you have a $20 billion fund and you're getting a 2 percent fee on it or $400 million a year, which seems like chump change to those that are managing them but sounds like real money in Omaha â if you're getting 400 million a year from that $20 billion fund, you can't start another fund with a straight face until you get that money pretty well invested.

Sync Video to Paragraph

It's very hard to go back to your investors and say, well, I've got 18 billion uninvested and I'd like you to give me money for another fund.

Sync Video to Paragraph

So there's a great compulsion to invest very quickly because it's the way to get another fund and another bunch of fees coming in.

Sync Video to Paragraph

And those are not competitors for businesses that Charlie and I are going to be particularly effective in competing with.

Sync Video to Paragraph

I mean, they â we are going to own anything we buy forever. The math has to make sense to us. We're not given to optimistic assumptions, and we don't get paid based on activity.

Sync Video to Paragraph

But I think it will be quite some time before â it's likely to be quite some time â before disillusionment sets in and the money quits flowing to these people that are promoting these. And whether they can continue to make deals will depend on whether people will give them lots of financing at what I would regard as quite low rates.

Charlie?

Sync Video to Paragraph

WARREN BUFFETT: We favor the businesses where we really think we know the answer.

Sync Video to Paragraph

And, therefore, if a business gets to the point where we think the industry in which it operates, the competitive position or anything is so chancy that we can't really come up with a figure, we don't really try to compensate for that sort of thing by having some extra large margin of safety.

Sync Video to Paragraph

We really want to try to go on to something that we understand better. So if we buy something like â See's Candy as a business or Coca-Cola as a stock, we don't think we need a huge margin of safety because we don't think we're going to be wrong about our assumptions in any material way.

Sync Video to Paragraph

What we really want to do is buy a business that's a great business, which means that business is going to earn a high return on capital employed for a very long period of time, and where we think the management will treat us right.

Sync Video to Paragraph

We don't have to mark those down a lot when we find those factors. We'd love to find them when they're selling at 40 cents on the dollar but we will buy those as much closer to a dollar on the dollar. We don't like to pay a dollar on the dollar, but we'll pay something close.

Sync Video to Paragraph

And if we really get to something â you know, when we see a great business, it's like if you see some â somebody walk in the door, you don't know whether they weigh 300 pounds or 325 pounds. You still know they're fat, right, you know?

Sync Video to Paragraph

And so if we see something we know it's fat, financially, we don't worry about being precise. And if we can come in, in that particular example, at the equivalent of 270 pounds, we'll feel good.

Sync Video to Paragraph

But if we find something where the competitive aspects are â it's just the nature of the business that you really can't see out five or 10 or 20 years because that's what investing is, is seeing out.

Sync Video to Paragraph

You don't get paid for what's already happened. You only get paid for what's going to happen in the future. The past is only useful to you in the extent to which it gives you insights into the future, and sometimes the past doesn't give you any insights into the future.

Sync Video to Paragraph

And in other cases, like the stable business that you postulated, it probably does give you a pretty good guideline as to what's going to happen in the future, and you don't need a huge margin of safety.

Sync Video to Paragraph

You should have something that â you always should feel you're getting a little more than what it's worth, and there are times when we've been able to buy wonderful businesses at a quarter of what they're worth, but we haven't seen those â well, we saw it in Korea here recently â but you don't see those sort of things very often.

Sync Video to Paragraph

And does that mean you should sit around and hope they come back for 10 or â you know, wait 10 or 15 years? That's not the way we do it. If we can buy good businesses at a reasonable valuation, we're going to keep doing it.
